title: The rooster crows (Luke 22:54–62)
hookLine: Peter swears three times he never knew him, then the rooster, then the look

cards: Pretending not to know someone. Laughing along. Keeping quiet when you meant to speak.
It can happen in a second, before anyone has decided anything. A courtyard in Jerusalem, in the middle of the night. Jesus has been arrested and taken into the high priest's house.
Mark says the others fled. But Peter, who walked on water, who said he'd go to prison and to death with him, follows at a distance.
He slips into the courtyard and sits down by a fire with the servants and guards, warming his hands.

teach.b: A servant girl looks at him in the firelight and says: this man was with him. And Peter, in the King James Bible: "Woman, I know him not." A little later someone else: you're one of them.
"Man, I am not." About an hour later, a third person insists: surely this fellow was with him, for he's a Galilean. And Peter says: "Man, I know not what thou sayest."
While he's still speaking, the rooster crows. Earlier that evening Jesus had told him exactly this, and Peter had said never.
Then Luke adds a detail no other Gospel has: "And the Lord turned, and looked upon Peter." Across the courtyard, their eyes meet. Luke doesn't describe the look.
The sources are silent. "And Peter remembered the word of the Lord, how he had said unto him, Before the cock crow, thou shalt deny me thrice. And Peter went out, and wept bitterly."
This story is in all four Gospels.

teach.h: PETER WENT OUT, AND WEPT BITTERLY.
teach.b: The first Christians could have left out the night Peter failed; all four kept it. Peter, the rock, the one with the keys, is also the one who said three times, I don't know him. And failure isn't where his story ends.
Tradition links the rooster on top of some church steeples to this night: a reminder to stay awake, and that even Peter fell, and was not finished.

how: Peter's denial is read in Holy Week in many churches, and it's sung in the Passion settings of Bach and others. Weathervanes shaped like roosters sit on some church steeples, especially in Europe.

o: a shepherd's horn calling the flock home
the rooster's call, as Jesus foretold to Peter
a soldier's shout raising the alarm at night

games.q: who said what — tap the pairs.
p: man, I know not what thou sayest
the Lord turned, and looked upon Peter

s: only one Gospel tells of Peter's denial
all four tell it. the early church didn't hide it.
Luke describes the look Jesus gave Peter
Luke says he turned and looked, and never says how. the sources are silent.
Peter was recognized as a Galilean
the third accuser said he was a Galilean. Matthew adds that his speech gave him away.

games.q: you're Peter, by the fire. twice you've said you don't know him. now a third person insists: surely you were with him, you're a Galilean. what do you say?
o: man, I know not what thou sayest.
get up and walk away without a word.
games.why: he denies it a third time, and the rooster crows. the Lord turns and looks at him, and Peter goes out and weeps bitterly.

practice: Bring to mind one old failure you still carry, a time you let someone down, or yourself, and look at it once, honestly, without replaying it; notice how long you've been carrying it.
Think of Peter weeping in the dark, whose story didn't end there, and say to yourself quietly: that happened, and I'm more than that. If you pray, you can ask to be forgiven and to forgive yourself.

wordCard.voice: Cock crow. The King James phrase for the sound that stopped Peter mid-denial, the third time, exactly when Jesus had said it would.

orig.note: Greek: a rooster. The bird that crowed after Peter's third denial.

carryVoice: Your line: even Peter. His story didn't end by the fire. Day sixty-seven, done.
